title: Spontaneous Regression of Cutaneous Epithelioid Angiomatous Nodule after Biopsy
content: Cutaneous epithelioid angiomatous nodule (CEAN) is a very rare vascular tumour that consists of epithelioid endothelial cells.[1] The pathogenesis of the tumour remains to be elucidated. Clinically, it often occurs on the trunk, arms and face and enlarges in a relatively short period.[12] We report a case of CEAN that disappeared after a biopsy.A 27-year-old female presented with a dorsal nodule that developed after scratching by a cat. She had no past history of systemic diseases. Her family doctor prescribed antibiotics, but they were not effective. She was referred to our hospital for evaluation of the nodule one year and four months after onset. Physical examination revealed a 5 × 7 mm solitary reddish nodule on her upper back [Figure 1a and b]. We performed an incisional spindle-shaped biopsy to make a correct diagnosis for complete resection. Histopathological examination showed a well-demarcated lobular nodule in the upper dermis, which was composed of sheets of epithelioid cells with vesicular nuclei and abundant cytoplasm [Figure 2a and b]. In immunohistochemical examination, the cells were diffusely positive for CD31 [Figure 2c], CD34 and ERG. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of CEAN was made. After the biopsy, two-thirds of the lesion had regressed. We performed surgical removal of the lesion one month after the initial biopsy. However, the lesional cells had disappeared and only inflammatory cell infiltrates were observed.Figure 1(a and b) A dome-shaped reddish nodule on the upper back before biopsy (a). The nodule after biopsy (before surgical removal (b)Figure 2(a–e) The lesion of biopsy, showing a well-defined border lesion confined within the dermis (a). Higher magnification of the lesion reveals a sheet-like proliferation of vascular endothelial cells and an inflammatory cell infiltrate composed mainly of lymphocytes and plasma cells (b). CD31 positive cells with vascular enhancement (c). The lesion of biopsy shows few CD8-positive cells (d). A surgically resected lesion shows hyperaccumulation of CD8-positive cells (e)Further immunohistochemical examination revealed that the infiltrating cells in the dermis were mostly positive for CD3 consisting of a mixture of CD4- and CD8-positive T cells. Comparing the biopsy tissue with the surgically removed tissue, the latter showed increased infiltration of CD8-positive lymphocytes [Figure 2d and e]. During a six-month follow-up period after surgery, there was no evidence of recurrence.CEAN was first reported by Brenn and Fletcher in 2004.[1] It is a relatively well-defined nodular lesion consisting of a sheet-like proliferation of endothelial cells with abundant acidophilic cytoplasm. Differential diagnosis includes epithelioid hemangioma and angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia. However, solid sheets of epithelioid endothelial cells with a poorly vasoformative growth are not the feature of these lesions. It has been reported that cyclosporine induced CEAN and that the lesions gradually resolved with discontinuation of cyclosporine. Although spontaneous regression of juvenile xanthogranuloma and lymphoma after a biopsy has been reported in some cases,[34] there has been no report of spontaneous regression of CEAN after skin biopsy.In the present case, there were numerous lymphocytes and plasma cell infiltrates mixed with histiocytes and intracytoplasmic vacuole formation of proliferating cells in the biopsy. Since most of the lesion was not removed at the time of biopsy, we speculate that the regression of the lesion was most likely caused by the external stimulus of biopsy that might have triggered infiltration of cytotoxic T cells, leading to spontaneous regression. Although the aetiology of CEAN is not clearly understood, it might be a reactive disorder caused by various stimulation. The course of CEAN may be associated with not only the persistence of the cause but also constitutional factors initiating cutaneous immune response. Further accumulation of cases and pathological analysis of the natural history of the disease are needed for CEAN.Declaration of patient consentThe authors certify that they have obtained all appropriate patient consent forms.
